title: No One Is Too Junior to Have the Best Idea
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that implied organizational status routinely suppresses good ideas from junior team members, who often fear stumbling in front of the people who lead them. Its central prescription is procedural: leaders should ask the least experienced people in the room for their thinking before anyone else speaks, deliberately reversing the usual status-driven order. The piece also recommends publicly recognizing junior team members' contributions when their ideas prove valuable, to reinforce that merit — not tenure — determines whose input gets weight. It takes a skeptical view of anonymous suggestion boxes, arguing they're a partial fix at best and can't replace an actual team norm that ideas are judged on merit.
points: The core prescription is procedural: solicit ideas from the most junior people in the room first, before status dynamics can suppress their willingness to speak.
Publicly recognizing a junior team member's idea when it proves valuable is named as a reinforcing mechanism that encourages others to contribute in the future.
Anonymous suggestion boxes are treated skeptically — useful as a starting point but not a substitute for an actual team norm that ideas are judged on merit regardless of source.
The piece frames over-reliance on anonymity as a quiet form of "suppression of open dialogue" rather than a genuine solution to status-driven silence.
quotes: Implied status in many teams inhibits proposals and ideas from anyone but leaders and those with deep subject-matter expertise.
Asking the most inexperienced team members for their ideas, opinions, and viewpoints before asking anyone else is a great way for leaders to open up the idea floodgates.
Good leaders also make a big deal of it whenever a valuable idea comes from a more junior colleague.
Over time, leaders who rely too heavily on anonymous suggestion boxes give into the suppression of open dialogue.
Good leaders remain curious about ideas and judge them on merit, not on status or experience.
